In Tunis we try to discuss divorce And dying but give up to lounge With rug merchants under a plum tree. From its corner the lamb’s severed head Watches the flies drink from its eyes And its fat disappear into the fire. The light rinses the edge of your sandal, The two wasps that ornament the blur Of screened window. My grandmother Would have loved a night like this. In the wind chimes I can hear her tea cart With its china rolling through Cook Street’s Stony yard one summer when I was always Thirsty, and she moved like a figure On a clock from my lawn chair to the cart, Or swabbed me with alcohol, or cut My hair with the straight razor. I was a week out of the hospital. Beneath my breasts an incision was crossed With stitches of surgical thread. The scalpel came so close it gave My heart a quick kiss. I nearly died. Years later I can still see the skin Flutter on the inside of my left breast And my heart limps like a great uncle Who, because he was a Jew and lame, Was dragged by cossacks across the steppes. prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Tunis, And, With

outputs.L1:
In Tunis, we try to discuss divorce and dying,  
but give up and lounge  
with rug merchants under a plum tree.  

From its corner, the lamb’s severed head  
watches the flies drink from its eyes  
and its fat disappear into the fire.  

The light rinses the edge of your sandal,  
the two wasps that ornament the blur  
of the screened window.  

My grandmother  
would have loved a night like this.  
In the wind chimes, I can hear her tea cart,  
with its china, rolling through Cook Street’s  
stony yard one summer when I was always  
thirsty, and she moved like a figure  
on a clock from my lawn chair to the cart,  
or swabbed me with alcohol, or cut  
my hair with the straight razor.  

I was a week out of the hospital.  
Beneath my breasts, an incision was crossed  
with stitches of surgical thread.  
The scalpel came so close it gave  
my heart a quick kiss. I nearly died.  

Years later, I can still see the skin  
flutter on the inside of my left breast,  
and my heart limps like a great-uncle  
who, because he was a Jew and lame,  
was dragged by Cossacks across the steppes.  

He became a friend asking a favor  
of a horse who ran so hard, so perfectly  
hard, that the green grass rose to meet him.
outputs.L2:
In Tunis, we attempt to speak of divorce  
and of death, then abandon the effort  
and sit idly with carpet sellers  
beneath a plum tree.

From the corner, the cut-off head  
of a lamb stares on  
as flies sip at its eyes  
and its fat melts away in the flames.

Light washes along  
the rim of your sandal,  
and touches the two wasps  
decorating the dimness  
of the screened window.

My grandmother would have cherished  
an evening like this.  
In the wind chimes, I hear again  
her tea trolley, its china rattling,  
moving through the rocky yard  
on Cook Street  
during a summer when I was never  
without thirst.

She passed, like a clockwork figure,  
from my lawn chair to the cart,  
or dabbed me with alcohol,  
or trimmed my hair  
with a straight razor.

I had been out of the hospital  
only a week.  
Below my breasts, a wound  
was laced shut  
with surgical thread.

The blade had come so near  
it seemed to brush my heart  
with a brief kiss.  
I almost died.

Even after many years,  
I can still picture the skin  
trembling inside my left breast,  
and my heart moves unevenly,  
like an old uncle  
who, being Jewish and crippled,  
was hauled by Cossacks  
over the steppes.

He turned into a companion  
begging kindness from a horse,  
and the horse ran so fiercely,  
so flawlessly fiercely,  
that the green field lifted itself  
to receive him.
outputs.L3:
The poem is set in Tunis, where the speaker initially seems intent on confronting weighty subjects such as divorce and death. Yet those difficult conversations gradually dissolve into a slower, more languid experience of place. Instead of direct discussion, the speaker spends time with rug merchants beneath a plum tree, absorbed in the suspended atmosphere of the market and the rhythms of ordinary life. This setting creates a tension between emotional crisis and sensual distraction, as though the speaker’s grief and fear can only be approached indirectly.

The poem’s imagery is vivid and unsettling. Details such as a lamb’s severed head, flies, fire, sandals, wasps, and wind chimes create a world that is both beautiful and decaying. These images mingle pleasure with threat: the shade of the plum tree and the musical sound of chimes coexist with blood, insects, heat, and death. The result is an atmosphere in which beauty is never pure or separate from mortality. The physical world presses intensely on the speaker, making the scene feel alive, but also unstable and haunted.

One of the most important sensory details is the sound of the wind chimes. Their ringing carries the speaker away from Tunis and into memory, recalling the speaker’s grandmother and a period of being cared for during a summer after hospitalization. The chimes become a bridge between present and past, between the foreign marketplace and the intimate space of family care. Through this sound, the poem shows how memory can be triggered unexpectedly by sensation, and how the body remembers vulnerability even when the mind tries to move elsewhere.

The speaker’s recollection centers on a near-fatal surgery. The memory is marked by the image of an incision beneath the breasts and by the frightening sense that the surgeon’s scalpel came dangerously close to the heart. This detail transforms the body into a site of trauma, survival, and fear. The wound is not merely medical; it becomes emotional and symbolic, suggesting how close the speaker came to death and how deeply that encounter remains embedded in the self.

By the end, the poem connects the speaker’s personal suffering to a broader history of ancestral pain. The lingering trauma of surgery is linked to the image of a lame Jewish great-uncle being pursued by cossacks. This ancestral memory expands the poem’s focus from individual injury to inherited vulnerability. The speaker’s scar and the great-uncle’s lameness echo one another, suggesting that bodily harm, fear, and persecution travel across generations. In this way, the poem brings together the immediate and the historical, the sensual and the traumatic, showing how private pain can be inseparable from collective memory.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores mortality, trauma, and memory through a series of associative movements rather than a straightforward narrative. It begins in a Tunisian setting, where an attempted conversation about divorce and death opens into a larger meditation on the fragility of human life. From this initial scene, the poem shifts into visceral, bodily images that suggest how grief and fear are not merely abstract ideas but physical experiences. Death is imagined not as something distant, but as something that presses against the body, interrupts speech, and shapes perception.

As the poem develops, it moves backward into childhood and recovery, suggesting that survival is never simple or complete. The speaker’s memories of illness or near-death experience remain alive in the present, resurfacing through sensation and image. These recollections show how the body remembers what the mind may try to organize or explain. The poem presents survival as a condition marked by vulnerability: to have lived through danger is also to carry its trace.

The poem also widens from personal memory into ancestral and historical suffering. Individual trauma is connected to inherited histories of violence, displacement, and endurance. The speaker’s experience is therefore not isolated; it belongs to a longer chain of pain and survival passed across generations. In this way, the poem suggests that memory is both intimate and collective. It exists in the speaker’s body, but it also reaches beyond the self into family, history, and culture.

Ultimately, the poem finds that near-death experience and inherited trauma remain bodily present long after the original events have passed. Mortality is not treated simply as an endpoint, but as a force that shapes identity, memory, and relation to others. Personal survival becomes inseparable from the histories one carries, the vulnerability of the body, and the violence endured by previous generations. Through its shifting images and associative structure, the poem shows that to remember is also to inhabit the ongoing presence of what has nearly destroyed, wounded, or formed us.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the style of a contemporary confessional travel lyric, set in Tunis, weaving together divorce, death, a lamb’s head, memories of a grandmother, surgery, Jewish ancestry, and a surreal image of a horse running across the steppes.
counterfactuals.output:
In Tunis I learn the color of endings:  
whitewash flaking from the medina walls,  
the sea lifting its blue sleeve  
as if to wipe my mouth.

My divorce arrives by message,  
a small bright coffin in my hand.  
I read it under an awning  
where men are drinking mint tea  
and arguing with the flies.

At the market, a lamb’s head  
rests on a silver tray,  
eyes clouded, lashes still tender,  
as though death had been interrupted  
mid-thought.

I think of my grandmother then—  
her wrists powdered with flour,  
her stories breaking open  
like figs in August.  
She said our people kept moving  
because history had teeth.  
She said the dead are not gone,  
only practicing another language.

In the hospital, years ago,  
they opened me neatly,  
a red doorway beneath the ribs.  
The surgeon’s hands entered  
like officials at a border.  
Afterward I woke with my body  
stitched into a new country,  
each breath a visa  
I was not sure I deserved.

Here, in the Jewish cemetery,  
names lean into salt air:  
Cohen, Levy, voices half-buried  
beneath bougainvillea and dust.  
I touch a stone and feel  
the old alphabet stirring—  
not belief exactly,  
but inheritance,  
that stubborn lamp  
passed palm to palm  
through exile.

My grandmother would have known  
what to do with grief.  
She would have salted it,  
boiled it, fed it to the family  
with bread.  
She would have looked at the lamb’s head  
and not turned away.  
Nothing was symbolic to her  
until it survived.

At dusk the call to prayer  
unthreads the sky.  
Cats slip through alleys  
like rumors.  
I walk past blue doors, brass hands,  
past children kicking a punctured ball,  
past my own reflection  
in a shop window—  
widowed from a marriage  
that is not dead enough  
to mourn cleanly.

And then, for no reason  
the mind will admit,  
I see a horse  
running across the steppes—  
black mane torn open by wind,  
hooves striking sparks  
from the dry earth,  
no rider, no saddle,  
only the terrible freedom  
of a body refusing its harness.

It runs through my grandmother’s kitchen,  
through the operating room,  
through the court papers,  
through the lamb’s blind stare,  
through Tunis with its lamps coming on  
one by one  
like souls being counted.

I stand in the foreign evening  
with my suitcase, my scar,  
my blood full of departures,  
and understand nothing  
except this:

even the severed head  
keeps the shape of hunger,  
even the dead carry names,  
even love, when it leaves,  
leaves hoofprints—

and somewhere inside me  
that horse is still running,  
not away,  
not toward,  
but across.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, image-rich poem that begins with two people in Tunis failing to talk about divorce and dying, then shifts into childhood memory, a near-fatal chest operation, and an ancestral story involving cossacks and a lame Jewish great-uncle.
counterfactuals.output:
In Tunis we sat under a ceiling fan that chopped the heat  
into dull white petals, and failed to talk of divorce,  
failed to talk of dying—  
two spoons cooling in coffee black as wet olives,  
two mouths full of sand and mint and the blue smoke  
of buses climbing the hill toward the cemetery.  

Outside, the sea kept unfolding its bright, official papers.  
Cats threaded the alleys like loose stitches.  
A boy sold oranges from a crate, each fruit  
a small sun with its fist clenched.  
You looked at the tablecloth. I looked at your hands.  
Between us, the word leave  
lay down like a dog that had been beaten  
and would not answer to its name.  

Then the city thinned, as cities do,  
and I was small again—  
knees scabbed, hair smelling of rainwater and iron,  
standing in my grandmother’s kitchen  
while onions hissed in fat  
and the windows sweated with winter.  
The radio coughed polkas and static.  
My mother’s dress moved around the room  
like a green lamp.  
In the yard, snow packed itself into the mouths of boots;  
the laundry froze into stiff flags,  
surrendering to no country.  

I remember the red tin soldier with one arm,  
the cellar apples shriveling in straw,  
the milk glass veined with blue,  
my father shaving—his face half-ghost, half-foam—  
and the little fear that lived under my ribs  
like a bird fallen down a chimney.  
It fluttered when I ran.  
It pecked at the dark.  
The doctors listened and frowned into me  
as if I were a locked cabinet.  

Then the white room. Then ether.  
Then the chest opened—  
not metaphorically, not like a flower,  
but with steel, with clamps, with the bright grammar  
of knives.  
My heart, astonished tenant,  
nearly handed back the keys.  
Blood climbed its red ladder and slipped.  
Someone said pressure. Someone said stay.  
A nurse, whose face I cannot remember,  
held my wrist as if it were a sparrow  
and called me honey from the far shore.  
I saw the lamp above me widen  
into a moon made of bone.  
I saw my own small body from above,  
stitched to the table by tubes and light,  
while death waited politely in its overcoat,  
snow melting on its shoes.  

But the old story came first, or after—  
time being a drawer jammed with knives—  
the story my grandmother told when the soup was gone  
and the dark leaned in to warm its hands.  
There were cossacks, she said,  
their horses black with sweat,  
their sabers carrying the weather,  
riding through the village like a broken fence of thunder.  
Doors burst. Chickens flew up like torn prayers.  
The synagogue burned with its beard of flame.  
And there was my great-uncle, the lame one,  
Jewish and stubborn, dragging his bad leg  
through the beet fields, through mud thick as judgment,  
his crutch knocking at the earth: let me in, let me in.  

He hid beneath a cart of cabbages,  
green heads piled over him like blunt saints.  
All night the horses snorted stars from their nostrils.  
All night the cossacks drank and sang  
with death sitting at the end of the bench,  
polishing its boots.  
At dawn, the village was a mouth without teeth.  
He crawled out alive,  
one shoe gone, one sleeve dark,  
his lame leg stiff with frost,  
and married, later, and begot, and begot—  
until my own ribs rose under the surgeon’s saw,  
until Tunis glittered with flies and salt,  
until you and I sat speechless over coffee,  
unable to say divorce, unable to say dying,  
while the past, that crippled uncle,  
kept dragging itself toward us,  
refusing, with every knock of its crutch,  
to disappear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a literary poem with no title, using long enjambed lines and vivid sensory details: rug merchants under a plum tree, flies in a lamb’s eyes, wind chimes like a tea cart, surgical stitches beneath the breasts, and a final visionary horse.
counterfactuals.output:
Under the plum tree the rug merchants unfold their small countries of wool,  
indigo rivers and rust-colored gardens unrolling into the heat while their thumbs  
worry the fringe like prayer beads, and the fallen fruit bruises open in the dust,  
sweetening the air with a purple rot that bees enter and leave as if carrying news.  

Beyond them a lamb stands trembling in the white noon, flies gathering  
in the wet black commas of its eyes, drinking the salt and shine there,  
and no one stops bargaining, no one looks away from the carpets’ buried fires,  
the reds deep as pomegranate skin split by a knife, the blues cold as wells.  

From the porch the wind chimes clatter and spill their thin silver weather,  
not music exactly, more like a tea cart rattling down a hospital corridor at dusk,  
cups ticking against saucers, spoons leaping softly in their drawer,  
the whole world preparing to offer some small comfort and arriving too late.  

I think of the body as a tent sewn shut after a storm, of surgical stitches  
beneath the breasts, dark little birds perched along the skin’s pale ledge,  
each knot a memory trying to hold the blood’s red door closed,  
each breath tugging at the thread with its warm animal insistence.  

Still the merchants lift their rugs to the light and the patterns blaze through,  
vines, moons, knives, lilies, the dust turning gold around their sandals,  
and the plum tree shakes loose one more overripe star into the grass,  
where ants assemble around its sweetness like monks around a relic.  

Then evening opens, immense and violet, over the market’s exhausted tongues,  
over the lamb blinking its burden of wings, over the chimes going quiet one by one,  
and from the far ridge, made of smoke, salt, and impossible flame,  
a horse appears—transparent, milk-eyed, mane streaming with constellations—  
stepping toward us as if out of a dream the earth has waited all day to remember.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an original poem that sounds like a 20th-century American lyric poet, blending North African travel imagery with personal illness, grandmother memories, and inherited Jewish trauma, ending on a strange pastoral transformation.
counterfactuals.output:
**In the Blue City**

I carried my fever through the medina  
like a second passport, damp and official.  
The alleys of Chefchaouen steepened into sky,  
blue walls rinsed in a light so clean  
it seemed to accuse the body.

Goats picked among the tins. A boy  
with mint on his breath offered postcards  
of dunes I had not yet seen.  
Everywhere, doors: studded, arched,  
painted the color of veins under skin.

At night the sickness opened its little shop  
inside me—brass trays, bitter roots,  
lamps smoking at the wick.  
My bones rang softly.  
I dreamed of my grandmother’s kitchen,

the sour steam of cabbage, the yellow oilcloth,  
her hands worrying dough into obedience.  
She kept sugar in a jar that once held nails.  
She kept silence in every other jar.  
When I asked about Europe, she wiped the table

until the pattern disappeared.  
What came down to me came slant:  
a name broken at the border,  
a train in the throat, black bread,  
the Sabbath candles hidden under a bed

where children learned to breathe without being heard.  
In Morocco the old men in the square  
moved their beads through their fingers  
as if counting the same dead  
by a kinder arithmetic.

I wanted to be only a traveler—  
dust on my shoes, coins warm in my palm,  
the Atlantic throwing its white animals  
against Essaouira’s walls—  
but the body is ancestral.

It remembers what it never survived.  
It folds the map along the wound.  
Even the desert, moonlit and immense,  
seemed less empty than inherited fear,  
that tent pitched inside the blood.

On the last morning, fever-thinned,  
I walked beyond the town  
where the blue gave out  
and the hills began their dry murmuring.  
A shepherd lifted his hand. The sheep stared

with their horizontal, unreadable eyes.  
Then something in me loosened—  
not healed, not forgiven,  
but altered, as water is altered  
when it accepts the shape of a trough.

My grandmother’s voice rose from the grass  
calling chickens that were not there.  
The stones sprouted wool.  
My shadow bent down on four legs to drink.  
And the sick wind grazed beside me, green.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal autobiographical free verse monologue in which the speaker recalls Tunis, a grandmother on Cook Street, recovery from surgery, a heart almost touched by a scalpel, and a great-uncle dragged by cossacks before becoming connected to a powerful running horse.
counterfactuals.output:
I remember Tunis as if I had invented it  
from fever and blue tile—  
a city rinsed in salt,  
where the sea kept lifting its eyelid  
and the white walls leaned close  
to listen to my blood.

I was not born there,  
or I was born there every time  
the afternoon broke open  
and the call to prayer threaded itself  
through the ribs of the streets.  
The sun walked barefoot on the roofs.  
Dates darkened like small hearts  
in the market’s shadow.  
I carried my name in a paper bag  
and the wind kept trying to read it.

Later there was Cook Street,  
my grandmother’s house,  
where the stairs complained in Yiddish  
or English  
or the language of old wood.  
She stood in the kitchen  
with flour on her hands  
as if she had been dusting the moon.  
Her soup simmered with warnings.  
Her curtains breathed.  
In her cupboards, the dead were folded  
like napkins for a holiday meal.

She would touch my forehead  
and say nothing,  
which meant: you survived something  
before you knew what survival was.  
Which meant: eat.  
Which meant: history is a dog  
sleeping under the table,  
and if you wake it,  
it may know your face.

Years after, I woke from surgery  
stitched to the world by tubes and light.  
The room was white enough  
to be a verdict.  
Machines blinked their small green eyes.  
My body was a country  
after invasion—  
bridges out, fields smoking,  
messengers lost in the rain.

They told me, gently,  
as if setting down a bowl of milk  
beside a wounded animal,  
that the scalpel had come close—  
so close—  
to my heart.  
Not metaphor, not song,  
not the red paper heart  
cut by a child for a classroom wall,  
but the fist of me,  
the engine in its dark garage,  
that stubborn tenant  
knocking all night.

I imagined the blade pausing there,  
silver and curious,  
like a fish at the edge of a cave.  
I imagined my heart turning toward it,  
almost touched,  
almost named,  
almost persuaded  
to open its door.

And in that narrow almost,  
my great-uncle arrived—  
not as a photograph,  
not as a family story polished smooth  
by retelling,  
but dragged through snow  
by cossacks,  
his boots leaving black commas  
behind him.  
The horses steamed.  
The sky was an iron pot.  
Someone laughed with a mouth full of winter.  
Someone prayed into his sleeve.

He was dragged and not ended.  
He was broken and not finished.  
His body, that torn flag,  
kept flapping in the empire’s teeth.  
And then—  
because blood has its own surreal arithmetic—  
he became connected  
to a powerful running horse.

Not mounted.  
Not leading.  
Connected.

A rope, a tendon, a vein of lightning.  
His terror entered the horse  
and the horse’s thunder entered him.  
Hooves struck sparks  
from the frozen earth.  
The cossacks blurred into crows.  
The snow rose upward, refusing gravity.  
My great-uncle’s heart,  
my grandmother’s kitchen,  
Tunis with its blue doors,  
my hospital bed,  
all harnessed themselves  
to that animal.

I felt it then—  
beneath the bandages,  
beneath the morphine’s soft green weather—  
a gallop not mine alone.

The horse ran through Cook Street,  
shattering the porcelain plates.  
It ran through the Tunis market,  
mane full of figs and sea wind.  
It ran through the operating room,  
past the stainless tray,  
past the stunned scalpel,  
past the surgeon’s gloved hands  
held up like pale birds.

It ran through me  
as if I were a field  
it had been promised  
before my birth.

Grandmother, I wanted to say,  
your soup has hooves.  
Your silence is a saddle.  
Your old house is moving  
down the street on muscular legs.

Great-uncle, I wanted to say,  
I heard the rope sing.  
I heard your breath  
become weather.  
I heard the horse carry us  
out of the century’s mouth.

And Tunis,  
Tunis of white glare and blue grammar,  
Tunis where the sea keeps washing  
the same wound clean—  
I remember you from my bed  
as if recovery were a harbor  
and I were arriving in pieces.

My heart, almost touched,  
kept beating.  
It did not forgive the blade.  
It did not curse it.  
It simply continued,  
a red horse in a locked room,  
running and running,  
dragging behind it  
the snow, the kitchen, the street,  
the salt city,  
the hands of the dead,  
and me—  
awake at last,  
astonished to be pulled forward.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
